text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Riksbank raps Sweden's commercial bank for keeping funds far too long in their internal clearing sytems in order to earn interest on the cash float. Transactions which take little time to process are not booked for several days.

- Women are not paid less than men, and reports of wage discrimination are a myth, a major new survey shows. What is true is that women are over-represented in jobs which pay low wages for both men and women.

- Cheap cafe programmes (a Swedish speciality in which the host and studio audience pretend to sit in a cafe and are entertained by minor celebrities) have increased their share of broadcast time by 227 percent over the past six years.
- A single dose of party drug ecstasy can cause depression, clinical anxiety, suicidal tendencies and spontaneous bouts of aggression, new studies show.
- Former Scandinavian Airlines System boss Jan Carlzon is building a new empire. He sits on the board of 18 companies and invests much of his time in his new travel group Transpool.

- Sweden hopes to avoid having to introduce tougher sanctions on airlines which bring immigrants to the country without the correct immigration papers. The issue has become a political hot potato since it affects the ability of refugees to leave their home countries.

- The Swedish political establishment is a fast track to career progress and higher pay. Over the past ten years, political top dogs have seen their wages rise far faster than normal state sector employees. Not only that, politicians have set up their own labour market, in the party and in related organisations.
- A serious lack of time and resources has made data from Statistics Sweden unreliable. This is an extremely serious problem, not least when national accounts are compiled.

- The power struggle for Swedish polymer maker Forsheda could turn out to be a good deal for Gunnar Bark, chairman of Forsheda's board. Bark stands to gain 10 million crowns from the bid made by Britain's TI group.
